ARIMA vs. ETS

The data is a set of information about retail sales at beer, wine, and liquor stores in the United States, monthly, measured in millions of dollars and not seasonally adjusted. The sample begins January of 1992 and ends in December of 2019.

library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)

liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  .gaps
  <lgl>
1 FALSE
liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly US liquor sales",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  )
liquor <- liquor |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales))

liquor |>
  gg_season(log_sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal plot: Monthly US liquor sales",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Log of millions of dollars"
  )

There is a definite upward trend in the data, with the size of the monthly swings increasing steadily as time progresses. This suggests that logs could be a good tool to stabilize the data. In the seasonal plot, the summer months as well as December seem to be peaks, while winter and fall are generally lower.

liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()

The ARIMA model selected is an ARIMA(1, 0, 2)(2,1, 1)[12] model, meaning the series is differenced once at the seasonal interval to try and achieve stationarity, but not at the regular interval. The ETS model selected is an ETS(A, A, A) model, meaning it has additive error, additive trend, and additive seasonality.

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()
liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .model lb_stat lb_pvalue
  <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 arima     120.         0

The residuals do not look like white noise, and we reject the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation in the Ljung–Box test.

liquor_cv <- liquor |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 120, .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id))

liquor_cv_fit <- liquor_cv |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(sales),
        ets    = ETS(log(sales)),
        arima  = ARIMA(log(sales)))

saveRDS(liquor_cv_fit, "results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

There are 97 forecast origins.

liquor_cv <- liquor |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 120, .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id))

liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
.model .type RMSE MAE
arima Test 81.43 65.65
ets Test 94.35 72.31
snaive Test 161.26 136.63

The first forecast is December 2001, and the last forecast is November 2019. According to the accuracy report, the ARIMA model forecasts more accurately.

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  liquor_errs$arimaliquor_errs$ets
DM = -2.9062, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.004042
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  liquor_errs$arimaliquor_errs$snaive
DM = -10.755, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value <
2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

The reported DM results are ARIMA versus ETS: DM = -2.9062, p-value = 0.004042; and ARIMA versus the seasonal naïve benchmark: DM = -10.755, p-value less than 2.2e-16.

We can conclude that the ARIMA model has the lowest forecast errors of the three models by a good margin, especially relative to the seasonal naïve model. If I were the liquor store chain, I would use the ARIMA model.

Forecast Combination

liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
.model .type RMSE MAE
arima Test 81.43 65.65
combo Test 85.19 66.77
ets Test 94.35 72.31
snaive Test 161.26 136.63

The combination ranks above ETS and the seasonal naïve benchmark but below ARIMA.

cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
[1] 0.8782934

If combining two models is most efficient when their errors are structurally different, then it makes sense that the combination did not beat the best model in this context. ARIMA and ETS have a correlation of 0.89, which is quite high, meaning they are structurally similar and so combining them does not yield a better model. Moreover, we know that ARIMA has less estimated loss on average than ETS, so combining ETS with ARIMA is more likely to add loss than be efficient.

VAR vs. BVAR

FRED-QD is a database of U.S. macroeconomic series variables measured quarterly. The variables used in this problem set are quarterly growth rates in percent or quarterly changes in percentage points. The sample ends in 2019 Q4.

qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))
growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

nrow(y)

There are 240 quarterly observations of eight variables. The first training sample contains 120 quarters, from 1960 Q1 through 1989 Q4, and the remaining 120 observations are forecast one quarter ahead from 1990 Q1 through 2019 Q4.

N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
      gdp      cons       inv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5130384 0.4598547 2.4927057 0.1956584 0.2084055 0.1988068 0.3902989 0.3610310 
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
      gdp      cons       inv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5693241 0.5268484 2.5212629 0.2277561 0.2069608 0.2153966 0.4973504 0.3789663

The VAR(1) model has a lower RMSE for all of the variables except the inflation rate. It is possible that the VAR(1) forecasts better because the additional parameters of the VAR(4) model may lead to data overfitting and worse forecasts when taken out-of-sample.

bvar_cv <- function(lambda) {
  pr <- bv_priors(hyper = "lambda",
                  mn = bv_mn(lambda = bv_lambda(mode = lambda, sd = 0.4,
                                                min = 0.999 * lambda,
                                                max = 1.001 * lambda),
                             b = 0))
  fc <- NULL
  for (T in origins) {
    fit_T <- bvar(y[1:T, ], lags = 4, priors = pr,
                  n_draw = 2000, n_burn = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
    x <- c(1, t(y[T:(T - 3), ]))         # constant and 4 lags of each variable
    fc <- rbind(fc, x %*% coef(fit_T))   # forecast of y_{T+1}
  }
  fc
}

set.seed(422)
fc_bvar_03 <- bvar_cv(0.3)
saveRDS(fc_bvar_03, "results/fc_bvar_03.rds")

set.seed(422)
fc_bvar_005 <- bvar_cv(0.05)

var_results <- tibble(
  Variable = colnames(y),
  `VAR(1)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var1),
  `VAR(4)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var4),
  `BVAR(4), lambda = 0.3` = rmse_by_var(fc_bvar_03),
  `BVAR(4), lambda = 0.05` = rmse_by_var(fc_bvar_005)
)

saveRDS(var_results, "results/var_results.rds")
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")
fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")

var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
Variable VAR(1) VAR(4) BVAR(4), lambda = 0.3 BVAR(4), lambda = 0.05
gdp 0.513 0.569 0.539 0.567
cons 0.460 0.527 0.486 0.495
inv 2.493 2.521 2.385 2.698
emp 0.196 0.228 0.211 0.315
infl 0.208 0.207 0.197 0.330
unrate 0.199 0.215 0.203 0.216
ffr 0.390 0.497 0.414 0.358
gs10 0.361 0.379 0.359 0.362

The BVAR(4) model with lambda = 0.3 beats the VAR(4) model for all variables. This difference results from the different criterion by which each model is estimated. VAR(4) simply minimizes OLS, whereas BVAR(4) introduces a prior that structurally alters the effect of lags, other variables’ lags, and distant lags, resulting in a different RMSE value.

Compared to the VAR(1) model, BVAR(4) with lambda = 0.3 performs worse in every variable except for the inflation rate and the GS10.

When lambda = 0.05, there is much stronger shrinkage and the model places heavier weight on its own prior assumptions. Moreover, choosing a model based on this sample is not a guarantee that it will perform well once it is out-of-sample. Selecting the model based on a low RMSE in this sample does not necessarily mean that it will have that same RMSE out-of-sample, as that could have just been a fluke.

e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  e_var4e_bvar
DM = 2.1366, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.03468
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
e_var4 <- actual[, "infl"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "infl"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  e_var4e_bvar
DM = 3.0265, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.003033
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Based on these tests, we see that the BVAR(4) model performs better than the VAR(4) model for GDP and inflation by statistically significant amounts, despite the RMSE values of both of these models being relatively close for these variables. This suggests that RMSE is not the sole indicator of a model’s forecasting ability, and that a wide range of components should be considered. It is more nuanced than 4.3b would suggest on its own.

Factor Model

The first row after the header contains transformation codes for the series. The data are transformed and restricted to March 1960 through December 2019.

md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)
[1] 718 122
tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
  INDPRO   PAYEMS CPIAUCSL FEDFUNDS 
       5        5        6        2

INDPRO and PAYEMS receive growth-rate transformations. The transformations of INDPRO and FEDFUNDS are likely different because they measure different economic components and therefore undergo different structural changes over time, requiring distinct statistical tools to stabilize them.

Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]

0.8415788 0.8404473 0.8390159 0.8219976 0.8028499 0.7903078 0.7778686 0.7768615

Based on the correlations, I would assume that the first factor measures overall economic activity, such as employment or industrial production. The strongest correlations related to the second factor, however, make me believe it is more related to prices and inflation, based on the FRED-MD index.

ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
  RMSE_AR   RMSE_FA 
0.6168431 0.5887272

We do get the same RMSE values for both! It would be cheating because of information leakage. This would incorporate future information into the forecast estimates of an early time period, which would not be available in real life.

direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month

  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  series   forecasts RMSE_AR RMSE_FA MAE_AR MAE_FA DM_pvalue
  <chr>        <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1 CPIAUCSL       349    2.11    1.89   1.58   1.35  0.000443

The factors do improve the forecast of 12-month CPI inflation, by 0.22 in terms of RMSE and 0.23 in terms of MAE, or about 10% of RMSE and 16% of MAE. We also know that the difference is statistically significant because the p-value of the Diebold-Mariano test is 0.000443, which is much smaller than 0.05, meaning we reject the null hypothesis of equal forecasting accuracy.

Reflection

The main thing that I learned from this problem set is that longer and more complicated models do not inherently produce better forecasts. For example, the VAR(1) model outperformed the VAR(4) model across multiple variables in terms of RMSE. At the same time, I also came to a better understanding that adding certain information or conditions, such as shrinkage, forecast combinations, and factor models can improve forecasting outcomes when proper care is taken. What these additions have in common is that they place some kind of structure onto the forecasting process, and this structure has the ability to capture useful forecastable information that is left out of the simpler models but may be slightly buried in the data. All in all, I think that I learned a bit more about the steps that we need to take in order to forecast accurately and carefully.
